title: REST contracts: pages, retries, and useful conflicts
outcome: Design bounded APIs and idempotent command handling with explicit retry behavior.
useCase: Ticket creation, payment-like commands, and large operational lists.
benefits: Predictable retries and manageable data loads.
drawbacks: Keys, retention, and mutable list ordering need explicit product rules.
cue: A retry is the same command only when you can identify it.

trace.title: Validate and authorize
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

An endpoint contract includes more than a URL. Define allowed input, authorization, response shape, errors, ordering, page limits, and retry semantics.

A list without a bound can turn an ordinary screen into an accidental bulk export.

Use stable ordering for pagination. Offset pages can shift when rows are inserted; a cursor can be more stable for an append-heavy feed.

A cursor must still be scoped to the caller and filter contract.

A retried create can duplicate a ticket. An idempotency key identifies one logical command.

Store the key with a request fingerprint and result under a database uniqueness rule. The same key with a different request should conflict.

A pre-check in a local map does not protect multiple service instances.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
A creates a ticket and commits, but the response is lost. A retry with the same key reads the saved result rather than creating a second ticket.

A different payload with that key receives a deliberate conflict.

Test simultaneous same-key requests, a timeout after commit, an invalid cursor, and permission changes. Define key retention; forgetting keys eventually changes retry behavior.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail:
PUT/POST method names alone do not implement idempotence. Cursor encoding is not encryption or access control.

A 200 containing an error object confuses clients.
